meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is no substitute for hard work'?
meta.ogDescription: Everyone quotes Edison. But no primary source ties this exact line to him — it’s an unsourced proverb pinned on a famous name.

answer.label: Not verified — an unsourced maxim pinned on Edison
answer.sourceLine: The sentiment squares with Edison’s well-known gospel of effort, but this exact wording turns up in none of his documented writings, interviews, or speeches. It is a floating one-liner — the same maxim is separately credited to football coach Vince Lombardi (“There is no substitute for work”) and to retail magnate Henry Sy — that later collections simply pinned on Edison’s famous name. His genuinely documented line about effort is different: “Genius is one percent inspiration, ninety-nine percent perspiration.”

source.excerpt: There is no substitute for hard work.
trail: The line is absent from the Wikiquote Thomas Edison page — it appears in neither the sourced nor the disputed sections, while his documented effort quote (“one percent inspiration…”) is traced to 1901, 1927 and 1932.

Quote Investigator’s study of Edison’s hard-work maxim documents a different line — “genius is hard work, stick-to-it-iveness, and common sense,” from his 1910 authorized biography — and never records a “no substitute” version.
The Edison Innovation Foundation does list “There is no substitute for hard work” on its quotes page, but with no source, date, or citation of any kind.
source.excerptNote: This wording is not found in any Edison speech, letter, interview, or authorized text. His documented statements on the theme run differently — e.g. “Genius is one percent inspiration, ninety-nine percent perspiration” and “The three great essentials to achieve anything worth while are, first, hard work; second, stick-to-itiveness; third, common sense.”
source.rightsNote: Because the exact wording cannot be tied to any identifiable first publication — it functions as an anonymous, oft-repeated proverb credited to several different people — no copyright status can be responsibly asserted. It is neither demonstrably public-domain nor traceable to a specific in-copyright work.

author.name: Thomas Edison
author.heading: About Thomas Edison
author.bio: Thomas Alva Edison was the prolific American inventor behind the phonograph, the practical incandescent lamp, and the first industrial research laboratory at Menlo Park, holding over a thousand US patents. He was famous in his own lifetime for preaching relentless effort over inspiration — his authorized 1910 biography records him snapping that “genius is hard work, stick-to-it-iveness, and common sense.” That reputation is exactly why unsourced hard-work maxims drift onto his name.

misattribution.heading: A maxim in search of an author
misattribution.intro: “There is no substitute for hard work” is the kind of clean, motivational line that attaches itself to any famous hard worker. It is most often hung on Edison, but the same words are credited elsewhere — and none of the credits comes with a primary source.

items.why: The line is absent from Edison’s authorized biography and from Wikiquote’s documented quotations; even the Edison Innovation Foundation lists it without any source.
The near-identical maxim “There is no substitute for work” is routinely attributed to the football coach Vince Lombardi, showing the same words circulate detached from any one speaker.
Quotation databases also credit the Philippine retail magnate Henry Sy: “There is no substitute for hard work. There is no such thing as overnight success or easy money.”

misattribution.truthLine: Edison genuinely championed effort — but his documented words were “Genius is one percent inspiration, ninety-nine percent perspiration,” not this tidier slogan.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Edison
lead: Edison built his public image on perspiration over inspiration, so a crisp aphorism about hard work feels like something he would have said — and that plausibility is exactly what lets an unsourced line survive as a quotation. The gap between “sounds like him” and “he is on record saying it” is where most magnet-name quotes live.

His real, traceable statements on effort are wordier and more specific, which is often the tell: genuine quotations carry the texture of a particular occasion, while floating proverbs are frictionless and interchangeable.
context.pull: It sounds like Edison. That is not the same as being Edison.
